tagline: From Page across the Navajo Nation, a highway beside sandstone landmarks.
intro: SR 98 runs southeast from Page into the Navajo Nation, crossing a stretch with few settlements beyond Kaibito. Beside the highway, Square Butte rises more than 700 feet above the surrounding land. The route received scenic-road designation after changes to its alignment in Page.

The state highway began in 1974 with the transfer of portions of Indian Route 22 to the Arizona Department of Transportation. Later, parts of the Page alignment became SR 989 and were relinquished to the city.

Begin at US 89 south of Glen Canyon Dam, follow the southern edge of Page, then continue southeast to Kaibito. Square Butte lies nine miles east of Kaibito. The highway meets Indian Route 221 before ending at US 160, the Navajo Trail.

moments.title: Kaibeto
moments.text: Kaibeto is a community on the Navajo Nation, 40 miles south of Page. Its school began in 1935, after local residents asked federal authorities for a school in the community. The first 45 students enrolled in a day school housed in stone buildings. Residents later requested boarding facilities; former army barracks became a boarding facility circa 1940. A request by Amos Singer in 1948 led to a new primary-school building, completed in 1954, with classrooms, dormitories and a cafeteria. The elementary and junior high divisions were consolidated in 1975, and Kaibeto Boarding School now serves grades K–8 under the Bureau of Indian Education.

moments.title: Square Butte
moments.text: Square Butte rises more than 700 feet above the land beside SR 98, east of Kaibito. Its Navajo name, Tsé Dikʼání, means “square rock.” The summit reaches 7,140 feet above sea level, with Entrada Sandstone over the Carmel Formation. Both formations were deposited during the Jurassic period. Runoff drains into Square Butte Wash or Potato Canyon and ultimately reaches Lake Powell, connecting this roadside landmark to the Colorado River drainage basin. White Mesa, two miles to the south, is its nearest higher neighbor. The butte stands on Navajo Nation land in northern Arizona.
moments.notice: The top of the butte is Entrada Sandstone above the Carmel Formation.

moments.title: Navajo Mountain pullout
moments.text: Navajo Mountain is a dome of igneous rock that pushed upward into sedimentary layers and lifted them. Those sedimentary rocks wrap the mountain’s core, with uplifted Dakota Sandstone at the peak. The summit stands at approximately 10,388 feet and is the highest point on the Navajo Nation. The peak lies in Utah, while its southern flank extends into Arizona. Its Navajo name, Naatsisʼáán, means “Earth Head.” The Dakota Sandstone was deposited during the Cretaceous Period; other rocks exposed on the mountain include the Jurassic Morrison, Entrada, Carmel and Navajo formations.
